title: Mother's cry 'really confused me,' officer tells inquest into disabled man's death
subtitle: A police officer involved in an altercation that led to the death of a mute, mentally disabled man testified at a coroner's inquest Tuesday.
article: As Charles McGillivary lay on the pavement turning blue and gasping for air, a police officer rolled him onto his side but did not perform CPR, an inquest heard Tuesday.

Raymond Kang had been a Toronto Police constable for two years on Aug. 1, 2011, when he and his partner were searching the Bloor and Christie Sts. area for a suspect who had allegedly violated his bail conditions.
The officers mistakenly apprehended McGillivary, 45, a mute, mentally disabled man who fell into medical distress after officers knocked him to the ground. A coroner's inquest is examining his death.

Kang testified Tuesday that he moved McGillivary to a "recovery position" on his side because he was worried the 270 lb. man was suffering from positional asphyxia, which occurs when someone's position prevents them from breathing.
Asked why CPR was not performed until paramedics arrived, Kang said he wasn't sure it was needed.
"It's not that I wasn't trying to do my best," he said. "I just wasn't sure if it was necessary at the time because he was gasping for air. You do it when there's no breathing."
The officer guessed that 50 seconds passed from the start of the altercation to the moment an ambulance was called. In fact, three minutes passed, according to police and Toronto EMS records.
McGillivary's handcuffs were removed after the officers realized he was in distress. Kang clapped his hands and tapped his cheek, trying to get him to "come to," he testified.

In a cell phone video shot by a bystander, McGillivary can be seen lying on his back before another officer arrives and helps to move him into a seated position. Kang said they sat him up because his tongue appeared to be swollen.

The mentally disabled man, who communicated only through sign language, was pronounced dead at Toronto Western Hospital. It was later discovered he had a pre-existing condition that resulted in irregular heart rhythm, hastened by the struggle with police.The Special Investigations Unit cleared the officers of any wrongdoing. Kang left the Toronto Police in 2012 and now works for GO Transit.

He testified that he and his partner responded to a 911 call about a suspect named Raymond Clarke refusing to leave a residence on Christie St. Clarke fled before they arrived, but the officers did not ask for a description of his clothing because they had a photo.
Kang admitted in cross-examination that this was a "mistake," but he said the officers still would have stopped McGillivary even though he was dressed differently.
"If we came across an individual who matched the photo, I still believe we would have stopped him," he said.

The photo of Clarke shows a heavy set man with dark eyes and a brown beard. McGillivary was also heavy, but had a grey beard and blue eyes. In addition, Clarke is about 6-foot-4, while McGillivary was 6 feet tall.
When the officers spotted McGillivary walking on Bloor St. W., Kang began to yell "Raymond, stop!" The man did not respond but abruptly switched directions and started to jog, Kang said.
The officer caught up with him on Grace St., where he grabbed one of McGillivary's arms. His partner, Const. Paul Gribbon, grabbed the other arm, and a "wrestling match" ensued, Kang testified.

As McGillivary tried to wrench away from the officers' grip, Gribbon used a "leg sweep" method to take him to the ground, as Kang held on to his arms to stop his head from slamming into the pavement, he said.
"That really confused me. It really did. It was in the back of my mind," he said. "We're still trying to deal with this individual and it made me confused."

The officer didn't know at the time that the woman was McGillivary's mother and closest companion, Ann McGillivary. She had been out for a walk that day with her son, with him striding several paces ahead.
Kang said her outburst made him "wonder" whether he had arrested the wrong person, but he didn't have time to question her.
"I was focused on the individual's state of health," he said. "There was no time to just walk away and conduct further investigation."
Although her comment stuck in his mind, Kang testified he didn't know he had arrested the wrong man until he read about it in a news article later that day.
"That's when it began to sink in more," he said.
